Node-level Domain Generalization on Graphs. Given a set of graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}=\{G^{e_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{E}|}] , where each graph [TeX: G^{e_{i}}=(A^{e_{i}},X^{e_{i}})] is sampled from a unique domain [TeX: e_{i}\in\mathcal{E}] and a domain [TeX: e_{i}] is defined as a joint distribution [TeX: \mathbb{P}(A^{e_{i}},X^{e_{i}})] . In each graph [TeX: G^{e_{i}}] , we denote [TeX: {A}^{e_{i}}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|\times|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|}] the adjacency matrix, where [TeX: \mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}] is a collection of nodes. [TeX: {X}^{e_{i}}=\{\mathbf{x}^{e_{i}}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|\times D^{e_{i}}}] represents the node feature matrix of [TeX: D] -dimensional vectors. [TeX: \mathbf{y}^{e_{i}}=\{y_{j}^{e_{i}}\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}^{e_{i}}|}] denotes node labels in [TeX: G^{e_{i}}] .

For node-level domain generalization, each graph [TeX: G^{e_{i}}\in\mathcal{G}] is associated with a specific variation in graphic topology [TeX: A^{e_{i}}] and node features [TeX: X^{e_{i}}] . The graph set [TeX: \mathcal{G}] is partitioned into multiple source graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}_{s}=\{G^{e_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{K}] where [TeX: K=|\mathcal{E}_{s}|] and [TeX: \mathcal{E}_{s}\subset\mathcal{E}] , and target graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}_{t}] with [TeX: \mathcal{E}_{t}=\mathcal{E}\backslash\mathcal{E}_{s}] . The objective is to maintain satisfactory generalization performance in node-level prediction accuracy transitioning from given source graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}_{s}] to target graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}_{t}] , with the condition that [TeX: \mathcal{G}_{t}] remains inaccessible during training.

Meta-Learning is an approach aimed at training a model over a range of tasks to be able to adapt to new tasks rapidly [54, 55, 20], where each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{i}\sim\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T})] associated with a data batch is partitioned into a support set [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{i}_{sup}] for the learning phase and a query set [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{i}_{qry}] for evaluation purposes. Meta-learning can be described as "learning to learn" because it involves finding a meta-parameter [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] from which one can quickly derive multiple optimized parameters [TeX: \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime i}\}_{i=1}^{M}] specific to individual tasks [TeX: \{\mathcal{T}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}] .

Model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) [39] is a notable gradient-based meta-learning approach that has demonstrated remarkable success in generalization. The core assumption of MAML is that some internal representations are better suited to transfer learning.

During training, the model first learns from [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{i}_{sup}] for each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{i}] and accordingly optimizes the task-specific parameter to [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime i}] with one or few gradient steps. The meta-parameter [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] is updated through query losses evaluated from [TeX: \{\mathcal{T}^{i}_{qry}\}_{i=1}^{M}] based on [TeX: \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime i}\}_{i=1}^{M}] .

where [TeX: \ell:\Theta\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}] is the cross-entropy loss for classification and [TeX: \alpha>0] is the learning rate. The goal of MAML is to learn an effective model initialization [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] using [TeX: M] training tasks, enabling rapid fine-tuning on the support set [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{t}_{sup}] of the target task [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{t}] to achieve optimal performance on [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{t}_{qry}] , where [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{t}=\{\mathcal{T}^{t}_{sup},\mathcal{T}^{t}_{qry}\}] .

Graph generalization using MAML leverages a similar GNN-based task distribution to accumulate transferable knowledge from prior learning experiences. However, the original MAML [39] assumes that all tasks originate from the same distribution, which hinders its ability to generalize across multiple domains [56, 57]. Additionally, GNNs can introduce noise information from task-unrelated edges, negatively impacting performance. As discussed in Section 1, GNN methods combined with structural optimization typically learn a static structure, which constrains the model’s ability to generalize to varying topology distribution shifts. To overcome these limitations, a cross-multi-domain robust algorithm is required, as we will discuss next.

Problem Setup. To address the problem of node-level domain generalization on graphs, where each domain is characterized by variations on both topology structures and node attributes, learning cross-multi-domain shared graph topology and node representation information is essential for capturing transferable knowledge across different domains. As shown in Fig. 2, a novel framework MLDGG is proposed in the context of meta-learning with two key components: a structure learner [TeX: f_{t}:\Theta\times(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{A}] parameterized by [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}] and a representation learner [TeX: f_{r}:\Theta\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}] parameterized by [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}] . The goal of MLDGG aims to learn a good parameter initialization [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}\}] across all given source graphs [TeX: \{G^{e_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{K},\forall e_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{s}] , such that the learned [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] can be effectively adapted to the target graph [TeX: G^{e_{T}},e_{T}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}] , which is inaccessible during training.

where [TeX: M\leq K] represents the number of tasks and [TeX: \oplus] is denoted as element-wise addition operation. [TeX: \text{GNN}:\Theta\times(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}] is a graphic representation function, parameterized by [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{g}^{e_{i}}] specific to the domain [TeX: e_{i}] . The representation learner [TeX: f_{r}] consists of a semantic encoder [TeX: E_{s}:\Theta\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{s}] , a variation encoder [TeX: E_{v}:\Theta\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{v}] , and a decoder [TeX: D:\Theta\times\mathbb{R}^{s+v}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}] . We thus denote [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}] as consisting of the parameters [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{s}] , [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{v}] , and [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{d}] , respectively, i.e., [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{s},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{v},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{d}\}] . Detailed setting and training of [TeX: f_{r}] is introduced in Section 4.2. [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{sup}^{e_{i}}] and [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{qry}^{e_{i}}] are support and query sets of the domain [TeX: e_{i}] , which are randomly sampled from the output of the semantic encoder [TeX: E_{s}] . Inspired by MAML, meta-parameters [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}\}] and task-specific parameters [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}^{{}^{\prime}e_{i}}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}^{{}^{\prime}e_{i}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}^{{}^{\prime}e_{i}}\}] are updated interchangeably through the bi-level optimization, using query sets [TeX: \{\mathcal{T}_{qry}^{e_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{M}] and support sets [TeX: \{\mathcal{T}_{sup}^{e_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{M}] , respectively. The learned [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] is further fine-tuned to [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}^{{}^{\prime}e_{T}}] using [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{e_{T}}_{sup}] from the target domain. The generation performance is then evaluated on [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}^{{}^{\prime}e_{T}}] using [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{e_{T}}_{qry}] .

Figure 2: An overview of MLDGG. Each source graph is viewed as a task. For each task, the parameters [TeX: \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}_{g},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}_{r}\}] of the structure learner ( [TeX: f_{t}] ), GNN, and representation learner ( [TeX: f_{r}] ) are updated via [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{sup}] during the inner update phase. Subsequently, the query losses [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{qry}] across all tasks are aggregated to update the meta-parameters [TeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{r}\}] in the outer update phase. To generalize to graphs in the target domain, the learned meta-parameters of the structure learner and the representation learner are further fine-tuned for adaptation.

The primary challenges of MLDGG involve modeling and capturing generalizable structure patterns across multiple domains, as well as disentangling domain-invariant semantic factors and domain-specific variation factors. To this end, the structure learner [TeX: f_{t}] is devoted to capturing shared structural information across domains while enhancing the comprehensiveness of representations learned by GNN through mitigating the adverse effects of task-unrelated edges (Sec. 4.1). Additionally, the representation learner [TeX: f_{r}] captures the invariant patterns of the truly predictive properties through the semantic encoder [TeX: E_{s}] by disentangling semantic and variation factors in node representations based on the causal invariance principle (Sec. 4.2). Finally, in Sec. 4.3, we integrate two learners within the meta-learning framework to capture transferable knowledge across various domains. For simplicity, in this section, domain [TeX: e_{i}] is simplified to [TeX: i] .

For graph data with both attributes and topologies, how to learn as comprehensive and rich node representation as possible is a problem that has been explored. One prevalent method is GNNs, which learns node representations through recursive aggregation of information from neighboring nodes. However, based on the model of the message-passing mechanism, small noise propagation to neighboring areas may cause deterioration of the representation quality. Therefore, we optimize GNN by learning high-quality graph structures. Further, we also explore the common structural pattern between cross-domain graphs to improve generalization ability. Despite GNNs having the capability to extract abstract representations for predictions, the representation may unconsciously mix up semantic factors [TeX: \mathbf{s}] and variation factors [TeX: \mathbf{v}] due to a correlation between them. So the model still relies on the domain-specific variation factors [TeX: \mathbf{v}] for prediction via this correlation. However, this correlation may change drastically in a new domain, making the effect from [TeX: \mathbf{v}] misleading. So we assume the representation of each node is disentangled into two factors: a domain-invariant semantic factor [TeX: \mathbf{s}] determining the label and a domain-specific variation factor [TeX: \mathbf{v}] independent of labels. [TeX: p(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] and [TeX: p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{s})] are invariant across domains, and the change of prior [TeX: p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] is the only source of domain change. MLDGG-ind. To improve the generalization of the model, we consider another case where [TeX: \mathbf{s}] and [TeX: \mathbf{v}] are independent, i.e., [TeX: p^{\perp}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})=p(\mathbf{s})p(\mathbf{v})] . Formally, the distribution [TeX: p^{\perp}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] exhibits a higher entropy compared to [TeX: p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] , which diminishes specific information of the source domain and promotes dependence on causal mechanisms for enhanced generalization. Under the conditional independence assumption, the [TeX: p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}))] can be turned to [TeX: p(\mathbf{s})p(\mathbf{v})] and [TeX: q(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{r})] can be turned to [TeX: q(\mathbf{s}|\mathbf{r})q(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{r})] in Eq. (10), which is denoted as [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{ELBO}_{ind}] .

We show the distributional assumption in MLDGG. For the prior [TeX: p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] , we use a multivariate Gaussian distribution [TeX: p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})=\mathcal{N}\left((\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})|(\mu_{s},\mu_{u}),\sum\right)] , where [TeX: \mu_{s}] and [TeX: \mu_{v}] are both zero vectors and [TeX: \sum=\begin{pmatrix}\sum_{ss}&\sum_{sv}\\ \sum_{vs}&\sum_{vv}\end{pmatrix}] is parameterized by its Cholesky decomposition [61]. For semantic encoder [TeX: E_{s}] and variation encoder [TeX: E_{v}] , we formulate their variational posterior distribution as Gaussian distribution with diagonal covariance structure, parameterized by neural network. For the decoder [TeX: D] , we adopt the Gaussian distribution [TeX: q(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{r})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}|\mu_{r},\sigma_{r}^{2}I)] , where [TeX: \mu_{r}] and [TeX: \sigma_{r}] are given by the mapping during reconstruct process. The semantic factor [TeX: \mathbf{s}=E_{s}(\mathbf{r})] is used to predict node label [TeX: y] , i.e., [TeX: \hat{y}=\hat{f}(\mathbf{s})] , where [TeX: \hat{f}] is a classifier. The variation factor [TeX: \mathbf{v}=E_{v}(\mathbf{r})] is independent of label. MLDGG uses both [TeX: \mathbf{s}] and [TeX: \mathbf{v}] to reconstruct representation [TeX: \mathbf{r}] , i.e., [TeX: \mathbf{r}=D(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v})] . For the prior [TeX: p(\mathbf{s})] and [TeX: p(\mathbf{v})] in MLDGG-ind, we adopt standard Gaussian [TeX: \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{s};0,I)] and [TeX: \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{v};0,I)] , respectively.
